title: The daily banis
hook: Nitnem means daily practice: set prayers at dawn, at dusk and at night

segments.voice: Yesterday, your simran, and a plan that fits your life. Your line was your five minutes. Did you keep them this morning? If not, there's always coming back. Day one hundred twenty-eight.

Most of us have a daily routine we barely notice. Coffee before anything. The same podcast on the drive. Checking the locks at night. Those small repeated things hold a day together, like the hinges on a door. Sikhs have a routine like this too, but it's made of words. At dawn, at dusk and at night, many Sikhs recite set hymns from the Gurus. Not new words each day. The same words, day after day, for years, until they're part of the person. Today we start a new stretch of the path: that daily routine of prayer.
screen: `COFFEE, PODCAST, LOCKS.` → `A ROUTINE MADE OF WORDS.` → `DAWN, DUSK AND NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The routine is called Nitnem. Nit means daily, always. Nem means a rule, a discipline, a vow you keep. So Nitnem is the daily discipline, and in practice it means a set of banis, hymns from the Gurus, said at fixed times. Bani simply means the word, the Guru's utterance. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada from the Akal Takht in Amritsar, lays out three times. In the morning: Japji Sahib, by Guru Nanak, then Jaap Sahib and the ten Savaiyas, by Guru Gobind Singh. Many Sikhs, especially those who have taken amrit, say five banis in the morning, adding Chaupai Sahib and Anand Sahib. In the evening, at sunset: Rehras Sahib. And at night, before sleep: Kirtan Sohila. Morning, evening, night. Three doors in the day, each opened with the Guru's words. Some Sikh traditions and jathas include a few more banis or slightly longer versions, and we'll come to that. Why the same words every day? Think of a path across a field. The first time you walk it, it's just grass. Walk it every day and it becomes a path, and your feet find it in the dark. Daily banis can work like that on the mind. Over years, the lines surface on their own: in traffic, at a hospital bed, at a wedding. And Nitnem isn't only for the devout few. Children learn it at home, grandparents keep it, and many Sikhs listen along to a recording on the way to work. Over the next ten days we'll meet each bani, plainly, one at a time.
screen: `NIT — DAILY. NEM — A DISCIPLINE.` · `MORNING: JAPJI, JAAP, SAVAIYAS.` · `EVENING REHRAS, NIGHT SOHILA.` · `A PATH WORN INTO THE FIELD.` · then, large: `MORNING, EVENING, NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Learn the three times, in your own day. Close your eyes. Picture your morning: where are you right after you wake? That's the first door. Now picture your evening, as the light goes and work ends. The second door. Now picture the moment before sleep, lights off. The third door. Walk through them slowly, one at a time: morning, evening, night. You don't have to fill them with anything yet. Just notice that each one is there. The bell holds the time.
Nitnem. The daily discipline: set banis of the Gurus said at dawn, at dusk and at night.
Your line: morning, evening, night. Today, at each of those three doors, pause for one breath and notice that you've crossed it. Day one hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Nitnem daily: Japji, Jaap and the Savaiyas (and often Chaupai and Anand) in the morning, Rehras Sahib at sunset and Kirtan Sohila before sleep, from memory, from a gutka or along with a recording.

myth: Nitnem means a new prayer every day
it's the same set banis, said daily, until they become part of the person.
the Sikh code of conduct names banis for morning, evening and night
the Rehat Maryada from the Akal Takht sets out the three times.
Nitnem is only for religious leaders
children, grandparents and working people keep it, often with a recording.

fork.setup: it's sunset and the day's work is done. which bani do many Sikhs turn to now?
fork.reveal: Rehras Sahib is the evening bani. Japji belongs to the morning, and Kirtan Sohila to the moment before sleep.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the daily discipline of set prayers.

trapdoor: what you thought: a daily prayer.
what it means: a set of the Gurus' banis said at dawn, at dusk and at night, the same words for a lifetime.
what a scholar hears: nem is from the Sanskrit niyama, a vowed observance; the Rehat Maryada fixes the banis for each time.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, Akal Takht, section on Nitnem

notes: The Rehat Maryada's list: morning Japji, Jaap, Ten Savaiyas; evening Rehras; night Sohila. Many Amritdhari Sikhs recite five morning banis (adding Chaupai and Anand). Confirm how the Keeper wants the three-versus-five framing.
'Some jathas include more banis or longer versions' (e.g., Damdami Taksal's longer Rehras) is left general; day 136 returns to it.
Nem from Sanskrit niyama: common etymology. Confirm.
